chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali from his father from Hammad ibn 'Uthman from al-Halabi from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said:
"There is no harm in you saying the Talbiyah while you are not in a state of purity, and in every state."

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: After mentioning what is obligatory for the Muhrim to do and avoid, which we will elaborate on in the chapter of what is obligatory for the Muhrim to avoid, if Allah wills: When he sees the houses of Mecca, and he is heading to it from the way of Medina, he cuts off the Talbiyah, and the boundary of the houses of Mecca is the 'Aqabah of the people of Medina. And if he is heading to it from the way of Iraq, then he cuts off the Talbiyah when he reaches the 'Aqabah of Dhi Tuwa. He narrated that.

key_terms.تُلَبِّيَ: Reciting the Talbiyah (the specific invocation of Hajj)
key_terms.عَقَبَةَ ذِي طُوًى: The boundary marker for those coming from Iraq
key_terms.عَقَبَةُ الْمَدَنِيِّينَ: The boundary marker for the people of Medina
key_terms.مُحْرِمٍ: One in the state of Ihram (sacred pilgrimage state)

ai.seo_question: When should a pilgrim stop reciting the Talbiyah upon entering Mecca?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes the permissibility of reciting the Talbiyah while not in a state of ritual purity (taharah), highlighting the flexibility of the pilgrimage ritual. The closing commentary by Al-Tusi clarifies the specific geographical boundaries—such as Aqabat al-Madaniyyin or Aqabat Dhi Tuwa—where the Talbiyah must cease upon entering Mecca, depending on the pilgrim's route. This reflects the scholarly tradition of linking ritual actions to precise historical and geographical markers of the sacred precinct.
